newsitem.title: USA: Australians show whiplash treatment effective.
newsitem.headline: Australians show whiplash treatment effective.

text.p: Baking painful neck nerve cells can provide long-term relief for those suffering from chronic whiplash injury, a team of Australian researchers reports in Thursday's New England Journal of Medicine.

The technique, known as percutaneous radio-frequency neurotomy, involves inserting an electrode into several points in the neck. The needle's tip touches the inflamed nerves that are sending the painful messages to the brain.
X-rays help position the electrodes and a radio frequency generator then creates a temperature of 175 degrees (80 degress C) at the tip, which seriously damages part of the nerve cells.

A team led by Susan Lord of the University of Newcastle tested the procedure by operating on 24 patients, whose neck pain had been documented by numbing the affected nerves with an injected anesthetic. In 12 of the patients, the radio frequency generator was used to destroy part of the nerve cells. But in the remaining 12, who served as the control group, the generator was never turned on.

Lord and her team then measured how long it took for the neck pain to return to 50 percent of its original strength. Among the volunteers given the full treatment, pain returned to half its strength in an average of 263 days. For those in the control group, it took an average of only eight days.

But results for individual patients were highly variable. The technique did not help three of the 12 people treated, after about three months the pain had returned in two more and a little over a year after surgery only one of the 12 reported being free of pain. Pain returns because the head of the nerve cell regrows and re-establishes its connection between the brain and the spinal cord.

"We found that radio-frequency neurotomy provided lasting, complete relief, but only in a moderate proportion of patients," Lord and her colleagues concluded. "Nevertheless, as shown in this study and previously, such relief can last for months to over a year, and if pain recurs the relief can usually be reinstated by repeating the procedure."

But the study also showed the power of placebos, and why their use is important to gauge a treatment's effectiveness. Among the 12 patients in the control group, six reported that their pain had disappeared. After about three months, that number had declined to three and after another three months or so only one continued to be free of pain.
